projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph E. Davis was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Joseph E. Davis. Joe served in the U.S. Army with the 522nd Quartermasters Regiment and the 405 2nd Quartermaster Truck Company. He served in the China Burma India Theater and his highest rank was T4. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Davis's home in Bedford, Ohio on January 20, 2006. Joe was 83 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: 1941? I was living at Oliver 2, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Explain what Oliver 2 is?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Oliver 2 is what some people call a coal camp. It was the name??they had the different corporations like the coal was owned and the property was owned by Oliver and Snyder Steel Company in Pittsburgh. And that's just like other places we had the Frick Coal Company. Different steel conglomerates, coal mines and coke ovens around for coal and steel to make-for coke to make steel.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was Oliver 2 near Pittsburgh?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Well, it's 52 miles back [Interviewed interrupted by banging or hammering].

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: As you can hear they're doing some work on the house?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: {Laughing}??During the day before they put the new highways in, it was roughly through the hills and curves, it was about 52 miles.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Fifty?two miles south of Pittsburgh?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yes. It was in southwestern Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So when were you born? What year?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: December the 16th, 1922.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Twenty?two, so you were almost 19?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: I was 20, 19??no I was 20 when I was??no, I was 19, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: ___ started at 18? What memories do you of the attack on Pearl Harbor on that day?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Well, I knew nothing. I come from a religious family and that was the first Sunday in December, and on the first Sunday, we usually spent the day in church, mother, father, sister, brothers. And we went to morning service and we had Sunday school, then after Sunday school, we had the communion service and after the communion service, we had what they call the BYTU, which is the Baptist Youth??wait Baptist BY??there's another word in there, but it's a training in religion. Then after that we had the 8 o'clock service at night. And we knew nothing of anything until we got home that night and then we--the first thing we heard on the radio was Pearl Harbor was attacked. And so we didn't think anything of it until we say oh Pearl Harbor. Well, who knew about Pearl Harbor in those days. Only people who traveling and knew or lived down there. So then the President Roosevelt gave his speech and this is the day we lived in??I can't quote the words that he said.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Day of Infamy?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Infamy, yeah. And then they started, I think the draft, and I was little too young. I think it was 18 to 25 I think the first draft. But then in 19??let's see it was 1941, I was already working in the mines. I graduated from high school in 1940, and I was already working in the mines, and they were increasing the production of coal and coke. And so I said, "Ooh, I be safe for a while," which I was. But then as they grew worst and drafting people, I said, "Ooh, I might have to go too." So in 1943??well, I started working in the mines in 1941, January of 41. And so I was calling around January of 43; I registered and then I went for an examination and in April, I was officially a soldier. I was sent to Fort Dix, New Jersey. And then??

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day of basic training?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yes, quite I remember when I first got to Fort Dix. We got there and we were screened and we had??well dinner was our first meal. So they had the big tables set up in the mess hall, and they marched us in by companies. There was two companies and one mess hall. And they served family style, big bowls of food sit on the table. And the first sergeant said, "Do not touch anything until we have the blessing." So he gave the blessing and then he hollered chow. When he hollered chow, all the food disappeared from the table, and I was used to waiting and you know food passed down the line and what not, and I didn't get any food. So I went to the first sergeant and I said, "Sergeant, I didn't get any food." He put his hands on his hips and looked at me and says, "You're in the army now, soldier." So I said, "Okay, Sergeant." So I went hungry that night. The next morning at breakfast, when they said the blessing and he said chow, I grabbed too. I don't know what I grabbed, but I grabbed a plate of something. And the guys say, "Hey, give me some, give me some." I say, "You give me some of what you got, and I'll give you some of what I got." And I'll never give you nothing. So, it wasn't nasty. I mean it wasn't nice, but if they would not share with me, I would take the whole plate and I would just eat off that plate. And while I was eating, I was messing over the food. And so they started sharing with me. So??but I would never forget he said, "You're in the army now, soldier." So from thereon, we went out??I was used to not exercise, but I been working, I had my exercise. I used to have to walk and sometimes almost a mile into the mine and walk out. And then during the winter, the license??we had an old piece of car and half the time I couldn't get the license plates on time, and we get them in June. You know??so we either road the streetcar, and if we come out of the mine before the streetcar start running, we had to walk home or ride around until the streetcar starts running. But went on until I was inducted and after I was inducted up at Fort Dix. After basic training, we had what we call "technical." And I was told when you're in the army, you never volunteer for nothing and to act dumb. When asked do you ever drive a vehicle, and if you said??they said if you said yes, they would give you a wheel barrel. And you work the wheel barrel. So, we was--we were--I was in the Quartermaster Truck Company, so they asked if I could drive, and I told them, no. So they sent me to class where I learned to drive. So this corporal I think it was. He explained to me everything on the dash was, and then we had a dry run through the shifting of the gears, one to five and five to one. And, so he says start up the truck. I turned the key and start it up, fed it a little bit of gas. He says, "You know you have to double clutch?" I said, "Yeah." So I put my foot on the clutch and I put it into second gear. They start us off you know with the second gear. And I got a little speed and he says, "Shift," so I double clutched and shift. He looked at me because I didn't scratch. You know I knew what I was doing, I had driven a truck before. Like you say, you never volunteer for anything in the army, you play dumb. So he--I shifted up and I shifted down to second. And he said, "You driven before haven't you?" I says, "Well, I driven a car." No, but you driven a truck. I say, "Well, a little bit." So, they pulled me out and made me a--put a band on my arm with two strikes on it, you know temporary. But anyhow I--then they put me through an obstacle course. They had barrels sitting there and you go in between, around, then you had to park, line them up. And you see one truck straight down the line. So he but he told me he kicked me out of class and put me--made me as an instructor. And then later on, I applied for the motor pool, you know work on the trucks after we got through our training, technical, I went into the shop. And I stayed there for a while until time to go on convoys. Then I rode with the direct guys, mechanics and the wrecker. So, then that's when we found out the drivers from the non?drivers. We hung around Fort Dix all summer, then early fall we went up to Camp Ruxley (ph), Massachusetts for training on the .50 caliber machine guns. They had the .50 caliber machine gun range and they had the ____axe firing over the ocean mostly. So [Interview interrupted by banging]. We came back--oh, on our way up to Camp Ruxley (ph), we drove all our supplies, ammunition, everything. And there's a slight breeze guys are pulling off, trucks are losing power. They says, "It won't run, it won't run." But we get in the truck, start it up, take off and shift up, and then there's a ____ yellow sleeper, we shift back [Interview interrupted by lots of banging]. They don't know they belonged in the fifth gear. But they didn't know because the trucks started slowing down, we bring them back to fourth. They slow down a little more, we bring them back to third. So they didn't realize that. So after--we had quite a few exchanges and vehicles while we were driving. When we got up there, it rained the day we got there, and it rained everyday. Some of us were slick. We were like the wrecker. We would get in back of the trucks instead of living in the pop tents. And if you touch it, it would leak. And our officers and non__ come kick us out, make us get out and get in our tents. But, it was quite an experience. Well, I came back from ____ there was death in my family, so I got a pass--emergency--I mean emergency pass you know the death in the family. So I get it. But when I was home, I got a telegram to report back for duty immediately. It was the day after the funeral because I wanted to spend a few days home with my mother, she being an invalid. And it was--I didn't want to come back, but she was blind in one eye, she couldn't talk, her whole right side was parallelized, and she was mumbling what--I says they want me to go back, but I'm not going back. She was motioning for me to go, go, go. So I packed up and I went. And Thanksgiving Day for dinner we had box lunch. We were on a train heading for Newport News, Virginia, and we were put in a stockade affair like. The prisoners of war were walking around outside the fence, and we were inside the fence. We couldn't go nowhere. But then we had a lot of fellows that were--lived down in Newport News, Virginia. They liked--wanted to go and say hi to their families. They couldn't. But these prisoners, they were out free, they were free.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Were these Italian prisoners or German prisoners?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Mostly Italian. Because the Italians, they were captured more readily than the Germans. The Germans were hard fighters from my understanding. So, we--then December 7, 1943, was less than nine months in service, we were shipped overseas to Casa Blanca. But we didn't know where we were going, but we ended up in Casa Blanca. And we spent there--time there through the holiday season. We found some--this red and green paper in the mess hall, and we kind of decorated--we didn't have nothing to put, pin anything up with, so they had this cactus with spikes on it about that high. So the building came down slanted down like this, and we took and, put the spike in the paper, stuck it in the wrapper, you know the wrapper, and then made a little Christmas decoration. But everybody had a good time until it come to Christmas night. Everybody but me. And we learned--we had a turkey dinner, turkey with all the trimmings and about that night, everybody was running towards the little tree, and I wasn't. I was sitting around, being from a family, close knit family, it was my first Christmas away from home. And I just lost my sister in November, and we were close because she was just a year older than I was. And we were, you know, buddies. We would run around together, always together. And the guys wanted to know, "You didn't get sick, you didn't?" I said, "No, why?" Well, I was heart sick, and I just couldn't--it just didn't seem like Christmas being away from the family and my sister just passing in November. But, it was a mess around there. The guys that got to the tree first--when they bent over, they squirted

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: And those that didn't get to the little tree, they squirted where they were, dropped their pants and squirted. But then they had clean up afterwards. But, then we went on a train they called the French Four 'N' Eights. They held 8 horses or 40 men, and went from Casa Blanca to Oran, and we stayed there for a couple of weeks. Then we got on another train the--most of the troops were unfortunate. They got in--they unloaded cattle and cleaned the manure out, and they had to march in. But I was with the Headquarters Company, and we had open cars where we had the--we hauled what they called TAT equipment to accompany troops. And we had loaded up and set it up when we got there. So then we made it to from Oran to Algiers, and we unloaded there, but the funniest thing was at Casa Blanca we had close order drill, Oran, we had close order drill, but when we got to Algiers, my little group we had unload the train, set up the equipment to the camp. And then we--I told the guys, since I was in charge of the group, I told them to hit the sack. It was about an hour before reveille. So I told them to hit the sack, and I would report them present and accounted for. So while we're out there, our company commander, he had a fit. He wanted to see the men; he wanted to make sure they were accounted the for. But they were--well I apologized to a degree because I was thinking of my men. So later on that morning after we had the--after reveille, we fell out--we had our chow, then they blew us out for roughing me, the camp commander because that was his camp. And one of the things was really nice, he told our officers he wanted to hear only three whistles a day, and everybody, you know, what the heck is this? He says he wanted to hear breakfast, lunch, and dinner, no close order drill or anything, just--and somebody made a crack about the company commander and myself, you know about blasting me out because I didn't have my men there. And I said, "Well, I didn't know nothing about this. I don't even know where I'm at. I don't know nobody here." I said, "But evidently this officer must have been close by and heard and overheard what had happened." But I just let it alone, but I always did--when I would we go on details, I always did look out for my men. There's one time I went begging to the officer's mess for some food because we were out on a detail and we got back late, and the mess officer for some reason or another didn't like me. When I went to him, you know, for food for my men, oh, you're too late, you're too late. So I went and seen this motor officer and he said, "You know you can't eat in the officer's mess hall." I know that. I just want some food, put it in buckets or mess kits and carry it out, and go to our barracks, under a tree some place and eat. I want some food. But I had a rough life considering, you know, but if you're not liked, you're not liked. And I wouldn't--you know really hard on the men. I would help the men. When we're on detail, I work with them. And the first sergeant, he come there one time we were on a detail, he told me I wasn't suppose to be swinging a mop. I was supposed to make my men do it. But this one time--well, this is back when we first went to Fort Dix {coughs}, we had the arena or something like that, you know it was a big building where they had sports and things, programs, and I had a detail to clean up. We weren't allowed to participate in it, but we had to clean it up. So I was there with the guys, and so they--I got chewed out by my first sergeant, and--so I threw the mop against the wall, leaning you know, watching the guys work. But then they went into the bathroom, and there was a stool. Around the stool, the top of it and the floor around it was as black as the back of that chair there. And so a lot of the guys they called you, even though you were temporary, they called you sergeant. They said, "Sergeant Dave, what are you going to do about this? I went and I looked, opened the door and looked at it, and I pulled the door shut, and I says, "Forget it." But you know I didn't say that {Laughs}. And so they went on and cleaned up, and the rest of the place was spotless but that one spot. So after we finished up, we went back into the company, and I guess ___ was in charge of the building. He reported to my company commander, I mean the sergeant, first sergeant, that I didn't finish the job. So my sergeant called me and asked me about it. And I told him the condition it was. He says, "Well, you're in charge of the group, you're suppose to make those men do." I says, "Sergeant, in the condition that that floor was in and that stool, I make no man do what I won't do myself." I said, "Now if I get down there with a toothbrush and start scrubbing, I would expect every man to get down there and start scrubbing with me. But that was too nasty, too dirty, and I wasn't going to make no man do because I wouldn't done it myself." So I think he, you know, the rest of the time, he had an iron out for me. After we got--well fast forward now. After we got to Algiers, this camp officer, he gave us a break, and after a few days, we got on a ship and went to Bombay. And we had a terrible storm on the way. We were in a convoy--well, the first ship we were on, we went over by ourselves. It was only seven days. We went departed the 7th of December and we landed in Casa Blanca on December 15th, eight days. But anyhow, after we got to Bombay, we caught a train and we ended up in Calcutta. I think we were on a train about a week. And it was quite a ride, and that was where we had our first touch of life because they told us don't eat anything, don't touch anything but what we had in all. So we were wondering why because people were different I would think. But on the train ride we go through different little towns, there would be a odd odor. We often wondered what it was until we came to a stop and we're going to be there for a while. So we decided to take a walk and had the little train station, walked around the train station, and one of the worst things I ever seen in my life was a corpse laying up there stripped down to the little G?string and decomposing. Then later on we found out there was a famine there in India and we were right there in the midst of the famine. We got there in the February of '44. But that was--and then we were sent to Camp Howrah (ph) and that's right outside of Calcutta, and we were taken to King George Docks and that's where we--when our trucks got there. We were at King George Docks. And then we drove from the docks to the warehouses, then from the warehouses, the time we get the call and haul supplies to the Dum Dum Air Base where they flew the supplies up over the hump. But, I was in line for Tech Sergeant, and then we had another guy came by way of the Pacific, and he was in line. So, I guess I wasn't one of those "kiss your butt" guys, independent and then I spoke what I thought within an inch of insubordination. But, when he got there with the trucks, I was reduced from--well we were both Tech Sergeants. I mean not Tech Sergeants, T4's [Interviewed interrupted by phone ringing].

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Is that your phone?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Somebody's.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Must be their cell phone.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: So, I was reduced from T4 to Private, but under the bottom of the order, I was promoted to T5. They told me I was going to drive a truck, and the guys were working seven days a week, 12 hours a day there for--and they were really pitching it for a while, and I said I wasn't going to drive a truck. What are you gonna do? So, I start--drove truck a few days, then I started coal working, go to the--I mean sick haul. So after sick haul for a time, somehow or another the government decided they were going to open, put some guys on temporary duty and they called it Base Section Second Echelon Shop. And what they were doing there we had--they would strip the trucks--they bring the trucks in and strip them down, go over the motor, go over the brakes, and lubricate, grease them, just almost complete overhaul. And I worked there as a tool room keeper. I had two tool rooms. And I had civilian employees, and there's one young man, he was bucks about 16 or 18 years old, but he spoke English fluently. So I chose him to be my interpreter, and then we worked til V?J Day. And but going--well I'm getting ahead of myself, but we had an officer who--well first of all the camp commander at Camp Howrah (ph), he was--anything you did it wasn't really in line, you went to the stockade. So there a couple of times we understand we were suppose to go up to the hills up to either Burma or Lido, but we didn't because or company was under strength. So we--the camp was all colored with the exception of white officers, and then but this one day, we saw this our camp commander in coveralls, policing the area around the headquarters. We couldn't believe it. Come to find out it was our camp commander was a lieutenant colonel, but then there was a full colonel had come in and replaced him. And it was the happiest days of our lives. Because this they tell me that this full colonel went up, took a convoy up to the stockade. And what are you in for? Off limits, you know just minor stuff and those that were in for more serious, he left them there. But he brought all of the guys that just minor back, and we had a bamboo back shed with fax roof. I know you know what those are, and they replaced them with buildings with tile roof. Fax roofs, any kind of bug you that you would name you could find up in there. So they--this guy--we didn't have any sports facilities. They built a platform where they had boxing and then they had--it was quite a difference this old colonel. He didn't allow anybody to salute him. You know you could nod or you know, but to salute officers some of them--but he was, he was a good guy. One of the days he was first there, he went to the mess hall and the guys told him the officers' mess was over there. He says, "I'm gonna eat this food." And that was the best thing that ever happened, a change in the food. Because there at one time--backing up--we went on a hunger strike at Fort Dix. And food was bad, bad, bad. So they knew that it, something was coming because the day we had the hunger strike, they had a beautiful breakfast. And the L Company ate first. They went in got the plates, trays loaded up, and then sat them all on the table and then walked out. And then we went in right after them. And we just walked straight through. We didn't even stop, you know because the trays were all in use, and the food all on the table. And then they wanted to know why we didn't eat that food. We gonna eat food that somebody else didn't want. Oh, so we were--both companies--we were punished, 15 miles out, no after lunch. We had a pretty nice lunch. And after lunch, they said fall out with full field pack, and they took us out seven and half miles and then brought us back. So after the next morning, we had breakfast. W--he told us to fall out with full field packs. They marched us out 15 miles, sat the truck out with chow then we come back. We had 30 miles that day. You talk about some tired, tired blistered feet. And they sent the officers?they were armed, side armed, and they sent ambulances out, you know because they figured that during the heat, some guys--we stumbled out--oh, then they--we marched 50 get 10. After the first march, the guys--we were out stepping and these blueberries all along the way, so we were out stepping and guys singing, singing old spirituals and everything. You know kept the spirits high. We never had no trouble. We went out that Friday, that Thursday night then Friday. That Saturday, they worked us--they wanted a swimming hole. There was a stream run through the property there. So they had details out with the guys with shovels and trucks, and they built a dam. Then Sunday we went out and worked a half day, and they brought us in. We showered, got our--put sun tans on and then we had retreat. And then after retreat, then we ate. And then they had a--like after retreat had like--this officer had some comments. And he said he had to take his hat off to us because we took our punishment like men. And we said, "Wow" {Laughs}. END OF TRACK 1

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: {Continues laughing} But it was a hard, hard--you had to piece this together. Couple of years ago, I might have had this story, you know, straighter than what I'm telling you.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: That's okay. It's all not out of sequence. But did you encounter much racism then when you?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Oh yeah. Oh, the racism, well, it started in my home town. See, I was born and raised in Oliver, which is about a mile outside of Uniontown, and Uniontown was racist. They had--you couldn't even buy a hamburger at Murphys (ph) that was the drug store, the bars and everything else. You know you were--and in Uniontown they had one street they called South Street. Everything people of color wanted they could get on that street. They had the bar. They had the little apartment buildings that they made into a hotel. They had the [Interview interrupted by drilling] they had the barber shop, the beauty shop, the restaurants, the bars. Everything that you needed, you find on that one street. But now they had another--this was downtown. But up in the east end where most of the people of color lived, they had little restaurants and what not. But then there's a [Interview interrupted by drilling] act theater. They had the theater called State Theater, and Cab Calloway was playing there one time, night. Anytime you went to the theater, whether it was a movie or what, you buy, you go in this door, buy your ticket and go out this door, then you go in another door and you go up, as we call it "king of Heaven", well up next to the rafters. And that's the only place you could sit. But, it was like that until way after the war.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: In the army was there much of a problem with racism?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Oh yeah. I mean the different camps--you see we were across the Hooghly River in Howrah (ph). Now, the other troops were in town, some were__ at hotels, others they had camps at easy access to the city. But we were--well we had drive--well Howrah--well yet, we had the Hooghly River. We had to cross the Hooghly Bridge every morning to drive from Howrah down to the bridge, across the bridge then up Strand Road to the docks. That's quite a leg. At one time there, they had these little Navy, Navy boats that they were running across the river to, thought they could save time and money. A lot of the guys didn't like the boats, and so they drive their--the time the boats were running, they were off they have to take their trucks around and go to camp. Yes, and then if you were in Calcutta, you had a hard time. Of course, all the--they had the Red Cross there. It was service of color. The workers were of color, and like we say we never had any of the stars come to our place.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You didn't get any USO shows or anything there?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: No. If there was any, we didn't know nothing about them. And even the [Interview interrupted by loud noise]. Even the women, Red Cross workers were of color. And I [Interview interrupted by loud drilling]. And I became friendly with one, but we couldn't--there was no time that we could get together except when she wanted to go some place, and she wanted a jeep and she wanted a driver, then she put in a request for a jeep and a driver and she would name me. And that was the only time we saw each other. She tried when I first met her--she tried and I told her I couldn't sit with her, and she said, "What's going to stop me from sitting with you?" You know they had officers here and these men here, so she would sit over there. The MP's would come and tell her that she couldn't sit here, the officers are on the other side of the isle, but like the old saying--we--then the first [Interview interrupted by loud drilling]. Oh, when I was going from, going to Fort Wayne, Maryland, we stopped in Washington D.C. from Dunbar, and there were two of us of color. I think there was ten, 12 of us, ten of them are white and the two color; and we went into this restaurant in Washington and this man [Interview interrupted by loud drilling]

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: You want to break for lunch {Laughs}?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: The corporal in charge marched us into this restaurant, and I guess the management was looking and he says, "I can serve them, but I can't serve those two." So I had to give this corporal in charge, you know he was--I don't know whether he was really--he wasn't dressed but just a group leader I say. He says, "Well, if you can't serve all of us, then you can't serve none of us." And he marched us out, took us to another restaurant and then went in there and there was a--we sat down, and somebody told this waitress don't wait on us. And that thing bothered me because she started crying and she said-- told us whoever told her that she said, "I'm going serve them because they're going to war and they might not come back." And that really touched me. I often wondered what happened to that young lady. Like I know she got fired.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: But anyhow, that was the beginning. I knew of racism at home.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Umhum, Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: But the funniest part of it at Oliver, you hardly knew who was of color until you look in the mirror. I walked to school, you visited each other's homes, like my mother taught some of the people in the neighborhood things about people of color and they taught us just like when I first got to CVI and I met Frank and there was a couple of people--my wife and I were the only ones of color in the Basia (ph), and so one day one of the ladies brought Frank some Cazals and he___ (3 seconds)--it didn't know what was in a bag and I reached down and got one and I said, "Oh my God." He says, "What's the matter? What's the matter?" He thought there was something wrong with it. I says, "No, I hadn't had any of this since I left home you know back in the 40's." He says, "You eat that?" I says, "Yeah I eat them." During the holiday season, my mother used to bake pastries and we were trade with the neighborhood, like Italians, Slavs, you know they have different pastries and what not and they would send little plates over to us and my mother sent plates over to them. And like you say, kids played together, went to school to together, and so it was really you know. So it was another lady asked us how do you like ____? I said I love it. I was born and raised on it you know. I liked a lot of soup. A lot of people love their soup. Mother had their soup and during the depression, well, we couldn't afford whatever, we just had the gardens and whatever food we had in the garden, made soup until mother had a stroke and she couldn't cook anymore and then she was on a special diet because doctor wouldn't--she couldn't-eat anything but lamb, fish and chicken meat. But it was until that time, and then like mother used to speak about three or four different languages, a little bit Italian, little bit of Slavic, little bit of Polish and like when we were kids you know. {Laughs - lots of noise in background} mother used to talk to us {Laughs} [Interview interrupted by lots of background noise].

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: They doing a thorough job you know?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yeah. That's the reason I wanted you, you know to come another day.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah. At least my machine works.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: So anyhow she--one day is a woman who called her Bubba or Starta (ph) Bubba which means old lady or grandmother and so this woman would come down the road she start talking to my mother and the kids on the other side of the road there was sitting on the porch and you know then mother ___ she would start talking, she sat for a while then start walking down the road you know and then she did something else and she turn back and start talking to my mother again, and my mother getting just as loud as she was you know. And she was speechless. Oh I didn't know your mother could talk like that. But it was nice living in the patches we call it. And everybody got along but.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: So you were still in India when the war ended?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yeah I was, yeah. We didn't get-let's see the war was over was September, October?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Yeah it was September when it officially ended. August was when they dropped the bombs.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Well we didn't get home until March.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Of 46?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yeah. The first of March, March 8th of 46. We landed in California. I think it was San Diego then we got on a ferry and went up to Pittsburgh, California. Then we had a night there in Camp Stolman (ph) and the next day we got on a train and started over to Camp Atterbury, Indiana. I was discharged at Camp Atterbury.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What was your reunion with your family like when you got back?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Well, it was really nice because this other fellow Addison Thomas, he--we went together. We left Uniontown in the streetcar together and went to Dunbar and to Calcutta and back and the same day, ended the same day. And so we worked together the whole time, but he passed two years ago. I was in contact with him, the only one I was really in contact with of the company. But in all it was a worthwhile trip. And like I often said when I was going to school I wanted to {Coughs}--Excuse me. I wanted to go through Africa but I didn't make it to the down in Africa but I was up at the French Morocco that was Africa. We were in Casa Blanca, Oran and Algiers, the top of it. But it was really a nice over to Bombay and Calcutta and then the surrounding little towns around there. But it was real nice.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Backing up a bit did you have memories of mail call? Did you get much when you were in the China Burma Theater? Did you get much in the way of mail or packages?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: I got a package every Christmas. I loved fruit cake and every year my father would pack a fruit cake and it was a special one. Remember the old A and P? A Ampage (ph) A and P fruit cake in a tin He buy a tin and they send it. The first time I got one I was mad as hell, excuse the language. Everybody wanted a piece of the fruit cake so then my great aunt she sent me one, but it ended up you know it just was in a box. It wasn't in a tin like the one my father sent. And we had crumbs and guys enjoyed it, anything from home. But yeah my father used to send me the Christmas of 41, I mean not 41 but 43, 44, 45 I had fruit cake. And the mail--as a matter of fact, I got very laxed in writing and my father sent me a--went to the Red Cross and had Red Cross contact me. He was wondering why I hadn't--if I was alright because I hadn't written anything. But I don't know why because I guess I was just running around and having fun. I stayed at the Red Cross most of the time and it was nice. I put it like this, I was one of the few soldiers that was really blessed because I saw no action. When we reached Camp Howrah, we locked our pieces up, and we didn't handle our pieces or see them until we were there 18 months. They took us out for a refresher course and then they locked them back up again until we come home. So I could not ask for a better couple of years of service than that.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Did you have any close buddies in the army?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Well the one that I went with. As a matter of fact we didn't know each other. But we did go to the same high school. Of course he was I think a year younger than I was. But he was with--he lived in a town on the other side of Uniontown, I lived on this side of Uniontown, but we went to the same high school called North Union Township High School. But we were together the whole time we were together. Then there was several of the guys in the motor pool, but we kind of hung and out together. But like I said this one platoon sergeant, he tried to be Mr. Big. When I was put on temporary duty, he gonna make me--assign me to--I mean first sergeant assign me to different duties like guard duty, KP, train orderly in all sorts of business and I went to this lieutenant who was in charge of us in the special duty group. He said, "You don't do anything but eat and sleep there. You don't have any duties." So this sergeant he get me up one morning dropped my--picked my bunk up and dropped it because I wouldn't get out of bed. It was on a weekend, Sunday. And then the next Sunday, I went and dropped his and he wanted to try to have me court-martialed. I wasn't a very well liked fellow because like I said I was independent and like the old saying go I didn't kiss behind.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: What do you think about your experiences during World War II? Does one vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yes, well more than one because while at India like the people bathing in the Hooghly River, the cows, the water buffalo, all that kind of stuff. Everybody live in the water. and then the burning gat, watching people brought their--of course we weren't allowed to take pictures but I do have a picture of just a little baby. The thing I couldn't understand is when Ghandi died, they had this great big funeral, they had full page ever him laying up there, but they didn't want us to take pictures at the gat where they burned him. But the guys, the short guys would stand there and the tall guys get behind them to take the pictures of the children. I got a picture of a little baby about like that upon a pile of wood you know that stuck with me. And then another thing I really loved was the Botanical Garden there. They have a beautiful Botanical Garden and then the banyan tree. The first time I ever heard I finally saw one and that's like the old saying goes, the largest tree in the world. It goes up and then it comes down, the roots go up and down. It's rally a sight to see. I really enjoyed and then I never been on a ship before or boat and the HMS Andes, the one at the time, we went over by ourselves alone. It was a fast, it was a luxury liner converted to a troop ship, then coming back I come back on the US--well the HMS Andes and then the what they call--I think it was a Dutch ship I guess it was, Jonathan DeWitt or something like that, and it was a foreign ship and then I came back on the HMS Andes, and I had a nice trip on that too because this Red Cross worker that I was friends with over there that was the ship she came over on, and she met a lot of the fellows there and all the ship crews all people of color, and so she associated with them and when she found out what ship I was coming back home on, she told the young man to look out for me. And I spent quite a bit of time in the skipper's pantry when the skipper wasn't around {Laughs}. And we played penuckle. I had a good time, but it was quite an experience. And then after joining the CVI Organization, I've been kind of busy because I was very--there weren't too many people of color in the organization. If they were, they didn't really attend the conventions.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Was that___ at Fort Dix?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: And that's your outfit? What was your outfit again?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: 522nd Quarter Master Truck Regiment. But then when they got ready to send us overseas, they changed it to--they broke us up into companies. We were really 452nd Quarter Master Truck Company and then the other regiment was 448th Truck Company, Quarter Master Truck Company. Yeah, so I like to say this--I didn't [Interview interrupted by drilling noise] I didn't know that people didn't about the CVI until I got into it

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: (Mafia) the organization you mean?

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yeah, the

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Sure. It's kind of an overlooked theater of the war.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: It's kind of an overlooked theater of the war

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: Yeah it is yeah. We call ourselves the forgotten soldiers. A lot of people never heard of us before and they said, "Where were you?" I said, "You saw the picture Bridge Over River Kwai didn't you? Well that was in Burma." And I said, "The Chinese War started in 1937."

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: 1937? I said we weren't fighting. I says, the United States wasn't fighting but we had some men over there fighting, the Flying Tigers, Chenault (ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: They were over there, but they just became veterans about four or five years ago because they were soldiers of fortune. They weren't U.S. Army Soldiers

sp.speaker: Thomas A. Swope
sp.p: Exactly. They were working for us.

sp.speaker: Joseph E. Davis
sp.p: So they said, "I didn't know that." I said yeah. Well I was in Camp Howrah some of them never been, seen or heard of Howrah and I told them, "What did you do?" I says we worked in docks, unloaded--they unloaded the ships onto our trucks and we drove to the warehouses and then we get a call they needed some supplies and we had to haul supplies to Dum Dum Air Base. Oh yeah I know where that is. You know they know--you say Dum Dum Air Base and everybody knew who Dum Dum was. And so they say oh I just--I didn't have much to do just take, run around and they said, "Well you were doing a job. If it weren't for you guys running around and hauling this stuff, we wouldn't got it." I felt better. END OF INTERVIEW
